title: Test out of Part D
crib:
These are the R behaviours the questions rely on.

- **An error message** reads `Error in <code> : <what went wrong>`. Before
  the colon is where R was when it stopped; after it is the problem.
- **A syntax error** — one with the word "unexpected" — means R couldn't
  read the line, so none of it ran.
- **Other errors** stop a script at that line. Everything before it has
  already run.
- **A warning** isn't an error: R finishes, but flags something.
  `suppressWarnings()` stops a warning being shown; it doesn't change what
  happened.
- **A column holds one type.** One entry that isn't a number makes the whole
  column text.
- **Comparing text with a number** compares them as text, character by
  character, the way a dictionary orders words. Letters sort after digits.
- **`as.numeric()`** turns text into numbers; anything that isn't a number
  becomes `NA`. **`na.rm = TRUE`** leaves `NA`s out of a sum or a mean.
- **`df$name`** with a column name that doesn't exist gives `NULL` —
  nothing — with no error. Names are exact, capitals included.
- **`summary()`** shows the smallest value, the quartiles, the median, the
  mean and the largest value.
- **`x[condition] <- value`** stores the value only where the condition is
  TRUE.
context:
Questions 7–12 use this data frame, `labs`. `k` is potassium (normal about
3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L); `creat` is creatinine in mg/dL (normal about 0.6 to 1.3).
One potassium sample was hemolysed.

```
   id         k creat
1 101       4.1   0.9
2 102       5.6   1.4
3 103 hemolysed   1.1
4 104       3.9   0.0
5 105       5.8  88.0
6 106       4.4   1.0
7 107       4.0   1.2
8 108       6.1   1.3
```

`summary(labs$creat)` gives:

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
  0.000   0.975   1.150  11.863   1.325  88.000
```

items.title: Reading an error
items.prompt:
```
Error in height * height : non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

Which part tells you what went wrong?

options.text: non-numeric argument to binary operator
options.feedback:
Right. After the colon is the *what*: one side of the `*` isn't a
number. Before the colon is the *where*: the code R was running.

options.text: height * height
options.feedback:
That's the *where* — the code R was running when it stopped. The
description of the problem comes after the colon.

options.text: Error in
options.feedback: That's just R announcing an error. The useful parts come after it.

items.title: A line R couldn't read
items.prompt:
```r
sbp <- c(118, 142 131, 156)
```

This gives `Error: unexpected numeric constant`. Does `sbp` exist
afterwards?

options.text: No — R couldn't read the line, so none of it ran
options.feedback:
Right. "Unexpected" marks a syntax error: R reads a whole line before
running any of it, and it couldn't read this one. (A comma is missing
after 142.)

options.text: Yes, holding 118 and 142
options.feedback: R never runs part of a line it can't read. Nothing was stored.

options.text: Yes, holding all four values, with 131 and 142 joined
options.feedback:
R doesn't guess what you meant. A syntax error means the line is
rejected, and nothing is stored.

items.title: What ran before it stopped
items.prompt:
```r
weight <- 70
height <- "1.75"
bmi <- weight / (height * height)
```

This stops with an error on the third line. Afterwards, which of these
exist?

options.text: `weight` and `height`, but not `bmi`
options.feedback:
Right. R runs line by line and stops at the first error. The first two
lines had already stored their values; the third stored nothing.

options.text: None of them — the script failed
options.feedback:
A script isn't all-or-nothing. The lines before the error ran and
stored their values.

options.text: All three, with `bmi` set to NA
options.feedback:
An error doesn't produce `NA` — it stops. The failing line stored
nothing, so `bmi` doesn't exist.

items.title: Where it broke, and why
items.prompt:
In the script from question 3, the error names `height * height`, on the
third line. Which line actually caused it?

options.feedback:
Right. The quotes made `height` text on the second line. R only
noticed on the third, when it tried to multiply. An error says where R
*noticed* the problem, which isn't always where it *is*.

options.text: `bmi <- weight / (height * height)`
options.feedback:
That's where R noticed, and the line the error names. But the formula
is fine; it was handed text. The cause is where the text came from.

options.text: `weight <- 70`
options.feedback: `weight` is a proper number. The other ingredient is the problem.

items.title: A fix that runs
items.prompt:
This gives `unexpected end of input`, because a bracket never closes:

```r
map <- (sbp + 2 * dbp / 3
```

An AI suggests closing it at the end: `(sbp + 2 * dbp / 3)`. For a
patient at 142/88, that gives 200.67. Is it fixed?

options.text: No — it runs, but the bracket is in the wrong place
options.feedback:
Right. MAP is (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3, so the bracket belongs after
`dbp`: that gives 106. Closing it at the end divides only the
diastolic part. The error went away; the mistake didn't.

options.text: Yes — there's no error now
options.feedback:
No error means R can run it, not that it's right. A MAP of 200.67 for
142/88 isn't plausible. The bracket belongs after `dbp`.

options.text: Yes — any closing bracket fixes it
options.feedback:
Any closing bracket stops the error, but where it goes changes the
answer. Here it gives 200.67 instead of 106.

items.title: Hiding a warning
items.prompt:
`as.numeric(c("12.4", "<5", "31.0"))` gives the warning *NAs introduced
by coercion*. An AI suggests wrapping it in `suppressWarnings()`, and the
warning disappears. Is the problem fixed?

options.text: No — "<5" still becomes NA; you just can't see the warning
options.feedback:
Right. `suppressWarnings()` hides the message and changes nothing
else. The real fix is deciding what `"<5"` should become — a clinical
call, not a coding one.

options.text: Yes — no warning means nothing went wrong
options.feedback:
The warning was the only sign that `"<5"` became `NA`. Hiding it
doesn't change the result: the middle value is still `NA`.

options.text: Yes — suppressWarnings() converts "<5" properly
options.feedback: It doesn't convert anything. It only stops the warning being printed.

items.title: Text compared with a number
items.prompt:
In the `labs` data frame (under **The data**, at the top), `k` is stored
as text because of the hemolysed sample. How many TRUEs does this give?

```r
labs$k > 5.5
```

options.text: 4 — including the hemolysed sample
options.feedback:
Right. Comparing text with a number compares them as text, so letters
sort after digits, and "hemolysed" counts as higher than 5.5. Three
real results plus one that isn't a number at all. Nothing warns you.

That's the right clinical answer, but not what R gives. With `k`
stored as text, "hemolysed" also counts as higher than 5.5.

options.text: An error — you can't compare text with a number
options.feedback:
R doesn't stop. It compares them as text, silently, which is what makes
this dangerous.

options.text: 8 — every value is text, so every one is TRUE
options.feedback:
Text is still compared character by character: "4.1" sorts before
"5.5", so it's FALSE. Only four come out TRUE.

items.title: Counting a second way
items.prompt:
To check the count, you convert to numbers first:

```r
sum(as.numeric(labs$k) > 5.5, na.rm = TRUE)
```

What does it give?

options.feedback:
Right. "hemolysed" becomes `NA`, `na.rm = TRUE` leaves it out, and the
three real high results remain. Getting a different answer by a
second route is exactly how you catch the first one.

That's the text comparison. Converted to numbers, "hemolysed" becomes
`NA` and is left out, so the count is 3.

options.text: NA
options.feedback:
`na.rm = TRUE` leaves the missing value out of the sum, so the result
is a number: 3.

items.title: Keeping the note
items.prompt:
Why is `labs$k_num <- as.numeric(labs$k)` safer than
`labs$k <- as.numeric(labs$k)`?

options.text: It keeps the original, so "hemolysed" — and the need to redraw — isn't lost
options.feedback:
Right. Overwriting `k` turns "hemolysed" into `NA` for good, and `NA`
could mean never drawn, lost or hemolysed. Keeping the original
preserves *why* a value is missing.

options.text: They're the same — both give the same numbers
options.feedback:
The numbers are the same, but overwriting also throws away the word
"hemolysed", which tells you the sample needs repeating.

options.text: The second is safer — fewer columns is tidier
options.feedback: Tidier, but it loses information: "hemolysed" becomes `NA` for good.

items.title: Reading the spread
items.prompt:
Look at `summary(labs$creat)` under **The data**. A normal adult
creatinine is roughly 0.6 to 1.3 mg/dL, and 1 mg/dL is 88.4 µmol/L.
Which values look wrong?

options.text: The 0, which isn't possible, and the 88, which looks like µmol/L
options.feedback:
Right. A creatinine of 0 is almost certainly a missing result typed as
zero, and 88 µmol/L is about 1.0 mg/dL — one result in the wrong unit.
Notice the median, 1.15, is normal while the mean is 11.86: a few
values are pulling the mean.

options.text: Only the 88
options.feedback: The 88 is one. But the minimum is 0, and a creatinine can't be zero.

options.text: None — the median of 1.15 is normal
options.feedback:
The median is normal, which is the clue: the mean is ten times
higher, so something is pulling it. Look at the minimum and maximum.

items.title: Fixing one value, and nothing else
items.prompt:
You want the creatinine of 0 to become a missing value. Which line does
that and changes nothing else?

options.text: `labs$creat[labs$creat == 0] <- NA`
options.feedback:
Right. `labs$creat == 0` finds the zero, the square brackets pick it
out, and only that value becomes `NA`.

options.text: `labs$creat <- NA`
options.feedback:
That replaces the whole column — a single value fills every row.
Every creatinine would be gone.

options.text: `labs$creat == NA`
options.feedback:
That only asks a question, and stores nothing. Comparing with `NA`
gives `NA` for every value, too.

options.text: `labs <- labs[labs$creat != 0, ]`
options.feedback:
That removes the whole patient, and their potassium with them. You
only wanted to mark one value as missing.

items.title: A count that's suddenly zero
items.prompt:
```r
nrow(labs[labs$K > 5.5, ])
```

This gives `0`, with no error and no warning. Why?

options.text: The column is `k`, not `K`, so `labs$K` is nothing
options.feedback:
Right. A wrong name gives `NULL`, silently, and asking a question of
nothing keeps nothing. A count of zero reads like a real result —
which is why a sudden zero is worth a second look.

options.text: None of the potassiums are above 5.5
options.feedback:
Three are. The capital `K` is the difference: there's no column by
that name.

options.text: The 5.5 needs quotes, because `k` is text
options.feedback: Quotes wouldn't help. There's no column called `K` at all.
